entities.summary:
Giovanni Cimabue, born Cenni di Pepo around 1240 in Florence, Italy, stands as a pivotal figure in the transition from the Byzantine artistic tradition to the nascent Proto-Renaissance. Often celebrated as the last great Italian painter working in the Greek manner and the first to break from it, his significance lies in pioneering a more naturalistic and emotionally expressive style that laid critical groundwork for the revolutionary developments of the Italian Renaissance. Operating primarily in Tuscany, Cimabue's oeuvre marked a decisive shift from the rigid, hieratic forms of medieval religious art towards a greater emphasis on human feeling and spatial illusion, thereby initiating a new epoch in Western painting.

Cimabue's key achievements include monumental panel paintings, such as the 'Santa Trinita Maestà' (c. 1280-1290) now in the Uffizi Gallery, which showcases a novel sense of depth and interaction among figures previously unseen in Italian art. His extensive fresco cycles in the Upper Church of the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi, particularly in the transept and apse, demonstrate a mastery of dramatic composition and emotional intensity, albeit heavily damaged by time. He also executed significant mosaic work, including a monumental Christ in the apse of Pisa Cathedral, illustrating his versatility across media and his engagement with major ecclesiastical commissions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cimabue served as a crucial transitional figure, bridging the Byzantine tradition with the burgeoning naturalism of the Proto-Renaissance, directly influencing the next generation of Italian painters, most notably Giotto.
